L6@P2: Calcium dynamics during trap closure visualized
L7@P2: in transgenic Venus flytrap
L8@P2: Hiraku Suda, Hiroaki Mano, Masatsugu Toyota, Kenji Fukushima,
L9@P2: Tetsuro Mimura, Izuo Tsutsui, Rainer Hedrich, Yosuke Tamada,
L10@P2: Mitsuyasu Hasebe
L11@P2: Nature Plants (2020) 6, 1219-1224
L12@P2: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41477-020-00773-1
L13@P2: The leaves of the carnivorous plant Venus flytrap, Dionaea muscipula (Dionaea) close
L14@P2: rapidly to capture insect prey. The closure response requires two successive mechanical
L15@P2: stimuli to sensory hairs on the leaf blade within approximately 30 seconds. An unknown
L16@P2: biological system in Dionaea is thought to memorize the first stimulus and transduce the
L17@P2: signal from the sensory hair to the leaf blade. Here, we link signal memory to calcium
L18@P2: dynamics using transgenic Dionaea expressing a Ca2+ sensor. Stimulation of a sensory hair
L19@P2: caused an increase in cytosolic Ca2+ concentration ([Ca2+]cyt) starting in the sensory hair
L20@P2: and spreading to the leaf blade. A second stimulus increased [Ca2+]cyt to an even higher
L21@P2: level, meeting a threshold that is correlated to the leaf blade closure. Because [Ca2+]cyt
L22@P2: gradually decreased after the first stimulus, the [Ca2+]cyt increase induced by the second
L23@P2: stimulus was insufficient to meet the putative threshold for movement after about 30
L24@P2: seconds. The Ca2+ wave triggered by mechanical stimulation moved an order of magnitude
L25@P2: faster than that induced by wounding in petioles of Arabidopsis thaliana4 and Dionaea.
L26@P2: The capacity for rapid movement has evolved repeatedly in flowering plants. This study
L27@P2: opens a path to investigate the role of Ca2+ in plant movement mechanisms and their
L28@P2-3: evolution.2
